::: {.lead}
At the end of every month, Huda writes a short report for the managers of
*Sunrise Company*. The numbers come from Rana's sales sheet in Excel. The
report is a Word document. On Monday, Huda shows the main points in a short
PowerPoint talk. Last month Huda typed the numbers three times, and one
number was wrong on a slide. In this lesson you learn to let the content
**move between the apps**: from Excel to Word, from Word to PowerPoint, with
AI help at each step and a check after it. At the end you share the
files and send an e-mail about them. In lecture 28 you start your
course project, which uses all three apps. Every section ends with a lab
task.
:::

## Key terms

{{< glossary office-suite office-workflow paste-options linked-object update-link heading-style slides-from-outline check-ai-output ai-use-statement >}}

## 27.1 One job, three apps

Each Office app has its own job (@fig-apps).

::: {.callout-important title="Definition 27.1 — Which app for which job"}
- **Excel** is for **numbers**: the data, formulas, totals and charts.
- **Word** is for **words**: a report or a letter, with headings, tables and
  pictures.
- **PowerPoint** is for **showing**: a talk with a few words and big
  pictures on each slide.

A **workflow across apps** is the order of the steps: the numbers are made
once in Excel, then they move to Word and PowerPoint. You do not type them
again.
:::

![One job, three apps.](images/three-apps.png){#fig-apps width=100%}

::: {.callout-note title="Example 27.1 — Huda's monthly report"}
1. Excel: `sales.xlsx` has the 24 sales, a summary table and a chart
   (lecture 25).
2. Word: `report.docx` has two pages, with the summary table and the chart.
3. PowerPoint: `talk.pptx` has three slides for the Monday meeting.
:::

::: {.callout-warning title="Common mistake"}
Doing the numbers in Word or on a slide with a calculator. Then the numbers
are not checked, and a change means typing them again. Do the numbers once,
in Excel.
:::

::: {.callout-note title="Lab task · Plan the three files"}
1. Open `march.xlsx` from lecture 25 (or the sales in **Link Lab**).
2. Write down what goes into each file: the Excel sheet, the Word report and
   three slides.

*Your result:* a plan of three lines, one for each app.
:::

## 27.2 From Excel to Word: paste options

When you paste an Excel table into Word, Word shows **Paste Options**
(@fig-paste).

::: {.callout-important title="Definition 27.2 — Three ways to paste"}
Copy the table in Excel (Ctrl + C). In Word, click **Home › Paste** and
choose:

- **Keep Source Formatting:** a Word table that you can edit; it does not
  change when Excel changes.
- **Picture:** an image of the table; you cannot edit the numbers.
- **Link & Keep Source Formatting:** a **linked table**. When the Excel
  numbers change, right-click the table and choose **Update Link**.

Charts have the same choices.
:::

![Three paste options.](images/paste-options.png){#fig-paste width=100%}

::: {.callout-note title="Example 27.2 — A missing sale"}
1. Huda pastes the summary table into the report as a link.
2. Rana finds a missing sale of bags: Bags changes from 78 to 98 JD in
   Excel.
3. Huda right-clicks the table in Word and chooses Update Link. The report
   now shows Bags 98 and a total of 375 JD.
:::

{{< sim file="sims/link-lab.html" poster="sims/link-lab.png" title="Link Lab: from Excel into Word" height="560" >}}

::: {.callout-warning title="Common mistake"}
Sending a report with a linked table to someone without the Excel file. The
link cannot update for that person. For the final copy, paste the table as
a normal table or a picture.
:::

::: {.callout-note title="Lab task · Paste the table"}
1. In **Link Lab**, do the two tasks.
2. Copy your summary table and your chart from `march.xlsx` into a new
   Word file `report.docx`, as a link. Change one number in Excel and
   update the link.

*Your result:* `report.docx` with a linked table and chart.
:::

## 27.3 From Word to PowerPoint: Slides from Outline

PowerPoint can make slides from the **headings** of a Word file
(@fig-outline).

::: {.callout-important title="Definition 27.3 — Slides from Outline"}
1. In Word, give the main points **heading styles** (lecture 7):
   **Heading 1** for each slide title, **Heading 2** for each bullet.
   Normal text does not go on the slides.
2. Save the Word file and close it.
3. In PowerPoint, click **Home › New Slide › Slides from Outline** and
   choose the Word file.
4. Choose a design, and add a picture or the chart to each slide.
:::

![Word headings become slides.](images/outline-slides.png){#fig-outline width=100%}

::: {.callout-note title="Example 27.3 — Two slides from the report"}
1. Huda makes "March sales" and "The best week" Heading 1.
2. "Total: 355 JD", "Paper sold the most" and "Third week: 112 JD" become
   Heading 2.
3. Slides from Outline makes two slides with three bullets in total. The
   long paragraphs stay in the report.
:::

{{< sim file="sims/heading-slides.html" poster="sims/heading-slides.png" title="Heading Slides: Word headings to slides" height="660" >}}

::: {.callout-warning title="Common mistake"}
Making text big and bold instead of using a heading style. It looks like a
heading, but PowerPoint does not see it as one, so no slide is made.
:::

::: {.callout-note title="Lab task · Slides from the report"}
1. In **Heading Slides**, do the two tasks.
2. In `report.docx`, add two or three Heading 1 lines with Heading 2
   points. Make `talk.pptx` with Slides from Outline.

*Your result:* `talk.pptx` with two or three slides.
:::

## 27.4 AI across the apps, sharing and e-mail

AI tools can help at each step. You check after every AI step
(@fig-workflow). Then you share the files and tell people about them
(@fig-share).

::: {.callout-important title="Definition 27.4 — Draft, check, share"}
1. **Excel → AI → Word:** ask for sentences about the checked totals (no
   personal data, lecture 23). Check every number with Excel, and edit the
   true sentences in your own words.
2. **Word → AI → PowerPoint:** ask for a short outline of three slides, or
   use Copilot in PowerPoint, if your account has it. Check every slide.
3. **Share and co-edit:** in Word, Excel or PowerPoint click **Share**.
   Choose **Can edit** for people who work on the file with you, or **Can
   view** for readers. Everyone works on one file in the cloud; comments
   and the version history show who changed what.
4. **E-mails and meeting notes:** AI can draft an e-mail with the link, or
   turn your meeting notes into a short list of tasks. Check names, dates
   and numbers before you send.
5. At the end, add an **AI-use statement**: one line that says where AI
   helped.
:::

![AI across the apps: draft, check, then move on.](images/ai-workflow.png){#fig-workflow width=100%}

![Share the files, then send a checked e-mail.](images/share-email.png){#fig-share width=100%}

::: {.callout-note title="Example 27.4 — The e-mail to the managers"}
1. Huda shares `report.docx` with Rana (Can edit) and with the managers
   (Can view).
2. Huda asks an AI tool: "Write a short e-mail to the managers. The March
   report is ready at this link. Total sales: 355 JD. Best week: the third
   week (112 JD). Meeting: Monday at 10:00."
3. The AI draft says "Best week: the second week." Huda corrects it to the
   third week, sends the e-mail, and adds the AI-use statement to the
   report.
:::

::: {.callout-warning title="Common mistake"}
Sending files as e-mail attachments to five people. Then there are five
copies, and nobody knows which one is new. Share one file with a link.
:::

::: {.callout-note title="Lab task · AI help, checked and shared"}
1. Ask an AI tool for three sentences about your totals (no personal
   data). Check each sentence with your Excel sheet, and put the true ones
   in `report.docx` with an AI-use statement.
2. Share `report.docx` with a classmate (Can view). Ask an AI tool for a
   short e-mail with the link, check it, and send it.

*Your result:* a shared report and a checked e-mail.
:::

## Case study: Office Relay

Huda's report passes from Excel to Word to PowerPoint. There are six jobs:
the total of the month, a table that must follow Excel, slides from the
report, an AI number to check, a report for a manager without the Excel
file, and an AI-use statement. The Game challenge of the interactive lesson
uses these jobs. In the mini-game below you choose the best way each time.

## Exercises

1. Which app is best for numbers, for a report, and for a talk?
2. Why do you make the numbers only once, in Excel?
3. Name the three paste options of this lesson.
4. Which paste option follows the Excel file?
5. How do you show the new Excel numbers in a linked table?
6. Why can a linked table be a problem in an email?
7. What does Heading 1 become in Slides from Outline?
8. What is the difference between Can edit and Can view?
9. When do you check AI output in a workflow across apps?
10. What does an AI-use statement say?

## Answers to the exercises

::: {.answers}
1. Excel, Word, PowerPoint.
2. So that the numbers are checked once and are the same everywhere.
3. Keep Source Formatting, Picture, Link & Keep Source Formatting.
4. Link & Keep Source Formatting.
5. Right-click the table and choose Update Link.
6. The other person does not have the Excel file, so it cannot update.
7. A slide title.
8. Can edit: the person can change the file; Can view: the person can only read it.
9. After every AI step.
10. Where AI helped, for example "the first draft was made with AI help".
:::
